The Master said, "The head of the monastery is utterly dull-witted; he has misled the three armies. Only when the bell was struck did he report [the time]. Is this not so?
The Main Section (*shōjūbun*): When the assembly has gathered, one returns directly to the abbot’s quarters; is this not the Dissemination Section (*ryūtsūbun*)?

Why then do you defer, saying, "For the sutras there are sutra masters, and for the treatises there are treatise masters"? Do you know where Yaoshan lands? When the Bodhisattvas and Dragon Kings move to bring down rain and moisten the earth, they veil their bodies by ascending yet more layers of clouds.
A monk asked National Teacher Longya, "How should one apply effort throughout the twelve periods of the day?
Longya said, "It is like a handless man performing a fist-punch. Shimen added, "Only when it is like a tongueless man knowing how to sing songs can it be accomplished."
The Master said: "Huiyun also has his way of speaking; it is like closing one's eyes and leaping into the Yellow River. Now tell me, among these three people, which one is on the right track?
If you can discern this, you will escape being hidden away in the realm of darkness."
Citing the Venerable Master Zhaozhou’s address to the assembly, he said: "The old monk has nothing other than the two meals of morning gruel and evening rice;

these are the occasions where the mind is distracted. The Master [Zhaozhou] said: "Great assembly, you do not know where this old fellow truly applies himself beyond his morning gruel and evening rice."
If you can examine this through and through, I grant that you may walk hand-in-hand with Zhaozhou.
But if you have not yet reached this point, even if you spend all twelve periods of the day in single-minded investigation, it will still be a matter of dualistic mental application.
Ultimately, how shall one bring forth that solitary, transcendent phrase? It is like the moon on a frosty night; let it fall naturally into the stream before you.
It is said that when Bodhidharma came from the West, he did not establish written words; he pointed directly at the human mind, so that one might see one's nature and become a Buddha.
The Sixth Patriarch said: "When the Patriarch spoke of 'not establishing,' he had already established it."

The Master said, "Ha! This is yet another commentary explaining a sub-commentary, which itself explains a commentary. While one seeks to uphold the direct pointing to the fundamental principles of the school, sixty kalpas pass in three lifetimes.
In the end, how is it? He struck the meditation staff once and let out a shout.
A monk asked Lingyun, "When the sovereign goes forth into battle, what then? Lingyun said, "Guo Pu buries [him] at Xiong'er.
The monk asked, "What is the meaning of this? Lingyun said, "Sitting, one beholds the white-clad heavens. The monk asked, "Where is he now? Lingyun said, "Right here."
[The Master] said: "Do not offend the Dragon’s countenance.
The Master said: "This monk disregarded his own peril and death to break through the ranks of the array. Lingyun joyfully encountered a favorable opportunity and led forth the imperial carriage.
If one examines this closely, it is a pity that he met [the opportunity] yet did not meet it."
The Master raised an example: A monk asked Zhaozhou, "What is the meaning of non-transmigration? Zhaozhou made a gesture with both hands as if flowing water.
The monk attained realization.
The Master said, "Zhaozhou’s spiritual pivot was swift and sharp, yet he exerted too much effort. That monk’s 'cracking and pecking' were simultaneous; I dare say [he has truly seen]."
Not yet thorough. Once, someone asked Yanfu, "What is the meaning of 'non-transmigration'? He simply said to him, "Put it down.
Do you understand? This will spare us from mutual entanglement."
Regarding Master Zifu: A monk asked him, "I have recently entered this monastic community and have already spent one summer here, yet I have not yet received the Master’s instruction.
I beg you for a single phrase. Zifu said, "Since I first took charge as abbot, I have never blinded anyone's eyes."
The Master said: "This monk sought but a single phrase, yet Zifu answered with two. Even so, he still says that he has not yet blinded people's eyes;
who has he deceived?"
The ancient verse says:

"When the World-Honored One was born from his right side and turned over, it was already strange enough; how could he have immediately understood how to dance the 'Three Terraces'? To set a model and establish a pattern is groundless."
How could one avoid the foul mouths of onlookers opening wide?

Ascending the seat to preach the Dharma, he occupies the throne of precious flowers; the true mark has always been inherently golden. Among the hundreds of thousands of disciples, who would not [be moved]?
Having seen it, what need is there to again apply purple-gold adornment?
At Vulture Peak he held up a flower;

at Vulture Peak his tongue was bound. He raised the flower branch; Kāśyapa could not evade him and displayed a smiling brow. Receiving the resonance and inheriting the void has continued down to the present day.
Day by day, the staff and shouts of sons and grandsons compete in their swift delivery.

Entering extinction at the Double Grove, the spilled water cannot be reclaimed; it fills the peaks of Zhugong. How could one, facing death, still rub his chest? To speak of non-speaking and existence brings about birth.
Extinction. It is all entrusted to a single dream within the spring breeze.

When the non-Buddhists questioned the Buddha, the whip’s shadow was shown not only to Ānanda; who knows that striking the void produces sound? At that time, it was perhaps not everyone who was truly capable.
The horse should envy the rising of the pure wind that unfurls the crimson banner.

When the head of the monastery asks after the illness, he brushes aside both the sun’s face and the moon’s face; it resembles the three before and the three after. The illness lies deep in the vital organs, where even a heavy torch would be of no avail.
Ai! How can the head monk Dou of the Hūn temple not feel shame?

When Mañjuśrī led his assembly to inquire after the illness [of the Buddha], they gazed upon that superior man in Vaiśālī; nine out of ten of them lost their spirits, yet it required only a single whole person [to save them].
Stone. It shatters the non-dual gate of the multitude of sages.
When the Mara King pursued Vajrasama Bodhisattva for a thousand years, he was far too ignorant. You say, "Who is Vajrasama? If you abide thus, do not speak.
Broken! Let this old fellow follow his own inclinations and harbor doubts.

He interrogated [Ānanda] on seven points regarding the mind, yet he interrogated the heavens beyond the heavens. A beam of light shot directly at Ānanda’s shoulder—Gautama is truly over-indulgent toward his son!
"Urged on, the eel is forced onto the bamboo pole.
Of the eight returns, the return of seeing is the final return;
after this return, there is no further returning. A solitary man wanders between heaven and earth. Last night, a tiger was caught by a leopard."
Bite! When the fur and skin have fallen away, the body reveals its original spots.

Do not seek the title of the sutra at the head of the scripture to recognize the fundamental reality; what is there to be sought within a stack of paper? Before the Sanskrit volumes are even opened, you must take it up.
Go! Avoid becoming one who merely traces the lines and counts the characters.
"A phrase, no phrase; a phrase, no phrase.
A vine leaning against a tree—this is much like a waterway opening in a parched sky. Just as the tree falls and the vine...
Withered! Look, look! Waves and surges pour forth upon level ground.
Xiangyan climbs the tree;
climbing the tree, he hangs his pivot to meet the Tiger’s Head. He knows for himself that spilled water can no longer be reclaimed, yet he is still able to laugh "he-he" face-to-face.
A laugh. He turns three springs into nine autumns.

Linji’s three blows of the staff—three rounds of painful blows striking the donkey’s waist—go straight to Gaoyuan, where he offers a full confession at the head of a rapid rapids, overturning the great boat.
Waves. Truly, one knows that when a house is wealthy, the children are arrogant.
To the assembly:
a separate transmission has branched out, swelling the stream of Caoxi. Myriad dharmas all come together, yet none are uniform. Leaves fall and return to the root; it remains so to this day.
Day. The partridge still cries out in Jiangnan.
A Dharma talk shown to the Chan practitioner Zongdu.

If Śākyamuni had not appeared in the world and Bodhidharma had not come from the West, the Buddha-dharma would have pervaded the world while those who discuss the profound mysteries would never open their mouths.
The ancients exhausted every means of compassion to open this direct path; it provides a standard for practice and conduct, serving as the model for later students.
Often, people do not trace back to their source; they wander outward in delusion and madness. To practice Zen and study the Way is to wander outward;
to seek words and chase phrases is to wander outward. To let go from the standpoint of emptiness is something rarely heard of in recent times.

When I first opened the hall at Yanfu, there were occasionally a few individuals who were also among those who had crossed over [to enlightenment]. In the autumn of the Xinwei year, I moved to Jiangshang, and the following winter, I ascended Xuefeng.
In the summer of the Jiashu year, I was a guest at Taicheng on South Mountain. This elder brother stands firm, dwelling within a boundless sea of merit; the eight winds cannot shake him.

Compared to others who are like fading blossoms or withered apricots, he is utterly incomparable. As the saying goes, "The misty leopard’s fur is so thick it never needs to descend to eat the birds in the courtyard";
he nurtures his courage solely to startle the world. If he can remain consistent from beginning to end in this way, the Old Barbarian (the Buddha) will have reason for hope.
To the attendant Shijing:
As for those who "part the grass and gaze at the wind," what is their ultimate goal? They must surely contemplate the cycle of birth and death;
they must clarify that single point which existed prior to both birth and Buddhahood. Yet, while intending to seek it in a place of stillness, they instead crouch in the midst of clamor. Furthermore—
One seeks him from amidst the clamor, yet he stands upon the ground of stillness. If one wishes to place him within the realm of non-action, he is once again a lively and agile entity.
How can one possibly grasp him? Only if one can realize that movement and stillness are of a single source.
This has been consistent throughout antiquity and the present. Polish it again and again; do not be constrained by the passage of time.

Naturally, the autumn waters will become clear and still, and the golden ripples will suddenly appear, illuminating mountains, rivers, and the great earth in all their myriad distinctions and thousandfold differences—though these arise merely from the differing natures of one's temperament.
There is a difference between those of sharp and dull faculties. Have you not seen how Old Dongshan answered the envoy from the Department when asked about the "pine tree":
"I repeatedly called for Little Jade, but it was originally for no reason; I simply wanted my husband to recognize the sound. At that time, Yuanwu was serving as his attendant.
As soon as he touched it, [the master] turned away. Thereupon, a verse on seizing the opportune moment was composed: "The golden duck's incense has faded around the emerald curtains;
Amidst the strains of pipes and songs, one is drunk and supported home. All that youthful grace and elegance— It lies solely in the moment of halting the needle and remaining silent.
This may indeed be called the style of the brilliant and swift. Since Attendant Jing sought a verse, I have written this general outline in response. If it were otherwise...
A nimble monk knows the flavor of the cauldron from a single morsel; Jingyi, examine this carefully.
The Way of Direct Pointing shown to the practitioner Ying does not involve language; as soon as it involves language, it becomes an indirect pointing. The ancients called this "attainment."
Moxi came from the West and was a diviner by trade. When he turned the divination board, all matters of good fortune, misfortune, regret, and shame were found entirely within one's own person.
By this it can be known: the mind is the mind inherently possessed by oneself; the Buddha is the true, natural Buddha of oneself.
The face is present before us, brilliant and flawless; yet we fail to investigate its source and merely gaze at a painted likeness.
Who would be willing to take a step back toward themselves and take the ancients as their standard? Have you not heard Zhaozhou’s words:
"Even if you vow not to speak for ten years, if you do not penetrate this Chan, cut off my head and use it as a dung shovel! This may be called "knowing the nature of medicines through much illness."
This experience was first transmitted to others. Yìngchán, do you still believe it? If you can truly believe it, then please accept it directly and break open the lacquer bucket.

To demonstrate true knowledge, one realizes that all speech and language belong to the school of Deva. Opening one's eyes, one enters the ranks of others; at the tips of every blade of grass lies the intent of the Patriarchs.
For a long time, they have been cast adrift in empty stillness. How pitiable are the followers of our school in this degenerate age, who often continue in such a manner.
Therefore, the single lineage of Shaolin has its life hanging by a thread; now that the worthy sages are hidden away, who can lend a hand?
The guest prefect Yizhen once served at Changgeng; his character is admirable—how could he lack blood beneath his skin?
To borrow the nostrils of an old monk to breathe out while remaining self-deceived and self-obfuscated—this is truly lamentable!

Rather than maintaining a single state of even-mindedness where one simply vanishes into oblivion, you should cast aside all "medicinal taboos" (preconceptions) and exert your full strength to grasp a single pivotal moment.
Otherwise, if you block your throat and recklessly force a single breath through, you will immediately see the vast, sweeping pure wind before Kāśyapa’s gate, and the [lineage] of Cao...
Upon the mountain stream path, white waves surge; naturally, it is luminous on all eight sides. The one true *dharmadhātu* is perfectly complete;
every head and every object is subject to its governance. When examined closely, how could this be a place of rest? Why?
Though Chang’an is pleasant, it is not a place for long-term dwelling.
To the Chan practitioner Zhen, surnamed Chisou (Dullard):
A single monk’s robe has come from the seat of Elder Xi at Mount Jin; his name is Zhen and his sobriquet is Chisou. He visited me seeking words to certify his dullness.
If this is how he attains his dullness, then he must truly have attained it. If he has truly attained his dullness, he must possess the eye.
Seeing like one blind, speaking like one mute, with a withered form and a soiled face, they are forgotten along with the world.
If it were otherwise, you should not take my words as the truth. Master Wang said: "Such dull-witted and ignorant people are rare enough in this world. Truly so.
Do not fail my expectation. Please, within the "tangled vines" of the ancients, silently reflect upon yourself and manifest the heart-seal of the Great Patriarch Longshou of Mount Ji.
Its form resembles the mechanism of the iron ox; its sharp edge was first revealed at Vulture Peak when Kāśyapa smiled.
This is that very seal. At Shaoshi, the subtle form possessed sharp edges; Shen Guang’s overturning of the halberd was also this seal.

Since then, it has been transmitted from patriarch to patriarch, with mind sealing mind. Sometimes they spoke of honey because of its sweetness; sometimes they spoke of sweetness because of its honey.
It is said that their mental capacity is like an iron ox. Yet, how can one know what form the mechanism of an iron ox takes? Such people are far too coarse in their Zen practice and inquiry.

Upon hearing mention of "a single thing," they must seek out the location of that single thing; upon hearing a "single seal" cited, they must investigate the dimensions of that seal’s circumference and diameter.
If they seek clarity through the corners of the mouth, they remain distant from the true shadow, appearing much like those who set out from Fuzhou only to end up elsewhere.

It is essential that you go to Chang’an; it is indeed very far away. Have you not seen how when Bai Zhang went for his second audience with Mazu, he thought there would be something extraordinary or some unique teaching to be heard?
Suddenly, his very heels were cut off by a single, majestic shout that left him deaf for three days and caused the seal-patterns on his skin to crack open.
Thus he came to sit loftily atop Mount Daxiong, where he gathered the most eminent talents—such as those of Mt. Wei and Huangbo.
All were trapped within a net. One man, upon hearing it, turned his body away from the touch; another, upon hearing it, went deaf and stuck out his tongue.
The rest of the sons could never match these two difficulties. This is what is meant by: "When one's views are equal to those of the teacher, one lacks half the virtue of the teacher."
"One who surpasses their teacher is alone fit to receive the transmission. Suddenly, after fourteen generations had passed, Miman appeared.
Sijong manifested his refined excellence on Mount Sam; our Way flourished for a thousand ages.

Directly descending as a single stream, only the two masters Chinsan and Jeong-sok played the *xuan* and *chi* flutes in alternation, their resonance still lingering in our ears. I recall the words of an ancient: "Do not dwell in the city."
In monasteries and temple compounds, one must seek out even half a person among those who dig by the side of their hoes in the deep mountains to serve as a companion for cultivation.
Alas, the demons are strong and the Dharma is weak; matters run contrary to one's wishes. It happened that there was the Elder De-xin of Jishan in Fuzhou.
Coming from a thousand li to surrender in sincerity, before even reaching the barrier defenses, his single foot has already crossed the threshold.

Whether the cauldron is large or small, or the handle of the ladle long or short—everything is seen through by him. As for "Mind": he is the direct descendant of Old Man Qian’an of former Jingci Monastery; water has its source and flow.
Once one knows that the seal does not depart from the mind, one will surely understand how to apply it according to circumstances. Thus it is said: "The Three Essentials."

The seal is opened before it is even struck; there is no room for deliberation, and the roles of host and guest are distinguished. Those who wish to be true descendants of Linji should act in this manner.
Thus he instructed his junior disciple, the Elder of Jiufeng.
In excavating a pond, do not shrink from the labor; when the labor is complete, the moon appears of its own accord. In responding to the world, one should observe the proper season;
when the season arrives, the principle manifests naturally. The Elder Jiupeng, named Fucheng, took "Moon Pond" as his own title.

Not long after he relied upon me, he successively presided over two mountains, and all remarked that the season had arrived and the principle was manifest—the pond was finished and the moon appeared. Yet they did not realize that it followed...
It is due to the ripening of karma that one has arrived at this state. If we discuss the fulfillment of one’s aspirations for a distant goal, there is a vast disparity between us.
It is like a misty leopard with glossy fur; it never stoops to eat the birds of the courtyard, for its cultivation of courage is intended to startle others.
Compared to this, how could I not feel ashamed? Nevertheless, many of the ancients were only able to penetrate Zen after they had already taken up residence in a monastery. Since—
It is said: "If one has a branch, one should grasp it; thus, diligence can compensate for lack of skill. Otherwise, on what basis could one command the respect of the assembly?
Furthermore, to regulate oneself with frugality and treat others with leniency, while diligently undertaking construction and maintaining the hall and kitchen—this is the constant duty of an abbot.

All the more so now that the Buddha-dharma is in decline; those who falsely claim to be teachers of men find themselves tossed by the winds of external conditions and easily succumb to worldly customs.
Those who wish to be revered by others must first establish themselves as independent and unconventional. One's son should be like Sun Zhongmou;
a junior disciple should resemble Baofu Zhuan. To leave a name for future generations—how can one not strive toward this?

Master Shizhen said, "The Master of the Dharma Repository, Kāśyapa, spoke extensively; the Dharma directly pointed it out. But tell me, what did he say? What did he point to? If one possesses superior faculties and sharp wisdom, they will understand upon a single spark.
For those of the next grade who strive with determination in their study, they may still cultivate this through habitual practice; how much more so for others!"

In recent years, teachers and friends have vanished; the Buddhas and Patriarchs are no longer heard of. The two paths of the heterodox and the orthodox are not distinguished, nor are the two terms "medicine" and "sickness" discerned.
Vast and aimless, people treat *tathatā* (Suchness) as a mere abstraction. Who knows that Zen is Zen, the Way is the Way, nature is nature, and the mind is the mind?
I recall fifty years ago, when I was spending the summer retreat at Cold Spring, sitting here on this side.
The Zen board has been struck; the bell for opening the lecture hall at Lower Zhu has sounded. Zen and doctrine contend for preeminence, and the lineages and expositions ride side by side.
I wonder if there have been any such tidings this summer? Master Congshan, who recently relied upon me at Xuefeng, was previously troubled by having to attend to the administrative office.

Lately, he has been confined to his seat due to illness, and I have not gone so far as to "draw legs on a snake" for him. Now that we are returning together to Zhejiang, we shall each go our separate ways.
Between them, there was not a single word. Fortunately, this was a fine instance of direct pointing. Yet, having come here to seek words, why do you create your own dull shackles?

Reflecting back on the masters of old, such as when Deshan entered Longtan’s gate and said, "The pond is not seen, and the dragon does not appear," Longtan replied, "You have truly arrived at Longtan; this is precisely where you should burn your scriptures."
Only when the paper candle is blown out does one suddenly glimpse the truth. By then, several critical junctures have already passed.
When Linji questioned Huangbo about the great meaning of the Buddha-dharma, he was beaten three times; this would have been the perfect moment for a reversal.

Yet, by the time Daguang enlightened him and he turned his head back toward the source, it was already eight *ke* (two hours) too late. Later, when the two masters employed blows and shouts, they were able to act within the realm where there is no Buddha.

He is honored as supreme; his power to kill or give life is free and unimpeded. He does not rely on the teachings of his masters, yet he serves as a model for those who investigate Chan throughout the ages, having thoroughly grasped the very core of the Buddhas and patriarchs.
His excellence is brilliant and acute, such that it can be known even without words. Should he encounter righteousness, he acts with courage, responding to the Way by thinking:
"Since he is a great man, so am I."
This demonstrates that the ancestral style of the Chan practitioners is vast and great; none but those of the highest faculties and fierce resolve can reach its depths.

Aside from the Seven Patriarchs of the Western Heaven and the Two or Three Masters of the Tang land, there have been no other old monks throughout the world who, since ancient times until the present, have possessed the creative power to transcend their own teachers.
I admire only a few individuals such as Linji and Deshan. As Huangbo said: "It is not that there is no Chan;
it is simply that there is no teacher. Take Deshan, for instance: he relied upon a single white staff and would strike even if a Buddha or a Patriarch came before him.
From the time of Tianhuang and Longtan onwards, who ever acted in such a manner? It was none other than the emergence of the School of Self-Nature.
Penetrating. Linji’s single shout was like a thunderclap in a drought; one could not strike it horizontally, nor could one strike it vertically.
This [lineage] has descended directly from Baizhang and Huangbo with a certain measure of authentic transmission.
Reaching him, it gave rise to waves that towered to the heavens and surged over the sun, so that by the eighth generation, upon reaching Dongshan, his fame shook even more mightily.

Within these past thirty years, you have suddenly become mute and passed away. Now that you have emerged from one forest monastery and entered another community, do not inquire whether there is Chan or a teacher;
simply be able to let go of everything, take the ancients as your model, and establish a firm and resolute mind.
With the power to uproot mountains, he suddenly breaks through like fire erupting from beneath the water or a cliff collapsing;
he transmits a spark of the lineage of the separate tradition that causes Kāśyapa to emerge from the Piṇḍola Cave and Dharma to return once more to the Eastern Land—
is this not truly admirable?
The essential pivot of the Chan school does not lie in leaving one monastery to enter another; nor does it require a monk to abandon one teacher to seek out another.
Thus, those who have merely caught a glimpse of the corner from behind a wall can come to understand it with perfect clarity.
If one further wishes to represent this through words, it would be like Dai Song’s painting of an ox—it may be lifelike, yet it is still not a living cow.
I have often heard the teachings of the Patriarchs: they are for adjusting the hands and feet of people of the present age; if your hands and feet do not stumble, there is no need for adjustment.
The teachings of the Buddhas and Patriarchs are prescriptions for treating mad sons; if your mind and spirit are not mad, there is no need for treatment. Only...
There are two urgent words that must be spoken to those who possess true understanding. Without clarifying one's own nature, there is no way to confront birth and death;

without comprehending what lies before one, how can one distinguish between the heterodox and the orthodox? Once the heterodox and the orthodox have been distinguished, you may roam freely in every direction.
Once you have clarified yourself, let things surge eastward or submerge westward as they may. Yet, as it is said by Samantabhadra:
"Not seeing a single dharma is a great fault. And as Yongjia says: "Not seeing a single dharma is the Tathāgata. How shall one penetrate these two distinct barriers?
Yesterday, having retired from affairs at Xueling, I was secluding myself on Censhan when the venerable Shu knocked at my door and spoke of the *Twenty [Verses]*...
It has been many years since we last met. I have just presented him with some *fuzi* (aconite) from Silla, and he has in turn recompensed me with cumin from his ship.
Since he is well-versed in knowing the proper timing, I have written this general outline to satisfy his request.
Praise for the appearance of leaving the mountains:
towering and lofty, solitary and remote. Abandoning the royal palace to dwell on the snowy peaks—clearly so cold that stars grew in his eyes. A banner.

Yet, having trodden upon the peaks of a thousand mountains, Avalokiteśvara contemplates with the ear and listens with the eye. The Way does not travel in vain; the valley does not respond in vain. Bestowing fearlessness—
Power. It extinguishes the disease of afflictions; it shares the same compassionate mind as all Buddhas and the same life of sorrow for all sentient beings.
Were it not for the Bodhisattva, who transcends both the mundane and supramundane realms, how could these two supreme excellences be attained?
Within the ocean of sounds and forms, he appears in accordance with the waves, piloting the *utpala* flower of a single leaf to open the skillful means of the Universal Gate.
On the shore of compassion at Mount Potalaka, no distance of hundreds of thousands of billions of lands exists.

When contemplating the sound of forms with the eyes, one hears; when contemplating form with the ears, one sees. Thus, the myriad dharmas are interfused and the six sense organs are mutually interchangeable.
At the time of such contemplation, the Buddhas of the ten directions all appear.

Bodhidharma traveled twenty thousand li to see the King of Liang. Without wind, waves arose; he could not find a single reed. He nearly drowned you—first there was no sage, second there was no recognition.
His loyal words were harsh to the ear, so he crossed north of the Yangtze. Entering the water, he saw a tall man. The King of Liang.
Now they turn pale with dismay. For a thousand ages, ten thousand ages, we shall vainly remember you.
Whether in the City of Longting or the Tuṣita Heaven, who among those who walk contrary to the flow or in accord with it does not know you? You have some stagnant wares that cannot be sold.
The treasury: wherever one encounters people, one picks it up at random.
Before even descending from birth, one has already set out on foot. Having bagged up heaven and earth, one handles them with ease.
A stretch of marsh, the flowing water white and vast; where has the staff ever reached it?
This tattered sack is most extraordinary; carried on the back and slung over the shoulder, one refuses to cast it aside.
Knowing only to enter the water to seek others, how can one avoid having one's heels bobbing and sinking as one crosses?

Hanshan (II): A single phrase lacks even a shuttle’s worth of artifice. When I engage in such reflection, where does my mind dwell? It is like the rain of the third watch falling upon the leaves of a banana tree.

At first glance, the steep cliffs stand like walls; their towering presence vies for height. In silent contemplation, one seeks the verse, yet alas, the golden-haired lion has run away—picked up by Shide.

Holding a fresh willow broom in hand, he lets it drop to sever all dust. Yet as he sweeps again, there is yet more; at the pine gate, ten li away, spring is like day. How can one urge oneself to apply the brush?

The itch within the belly is difficult to restrain; turning the head and looking back again and again, one does not know— (Note: The final phrase "不知" (does not know) is left open-ended, suggesting a state of non-attainment or the ineffable nature of the realization.)
The white elephant is lost;
the morning sun pierces through the tattered robe, an inch of iron held in hand.
Transverse and vertical penetration—where it cannot be pierced through, the sun’s orb rises in the sky.
Facing the moon, I finished the remaining sutras;
the black beans have not yet sprouted. Counting them morning and counting them evening, when my eyes opened, the full moon was right before my door.
I praised the image of True Awakening and transformed the people of Jiangbu.
He consumed the fierce and pungent [teachings] of Deshan; he endured the pressing scrutiny of his fellow practitioners.
He swept away all conceptual entanglements until, directly, fire erupted from beneath the water—*alala!* This is what is called a Bodhisattva of True Awakening.
True Awakening:
Deshan preserves its head; Yantou inserts its tail. Forced together into a single old cat, its two eyes glare and it has no teeth. Heh!

Mañjuśrī was appointed as the teacher by the seven Buddhas; the Dharma King hailed him as his son. Throughout the unfolding of the five periods of teaching, he assisted and supported from beginning to end.

While the World-Honored One constantly practiced samādhi, Mañjuśrī eloquently expounded the teachings with a smile. He manifested hundreds of thousands of wondrous forms for the Dragon Girl, and Kāśyapa...
The mallet could not lift him. He declared, "I am truly Mañjuśrī; who else could be my companion?
Vimalakīrti, well-versed in the protocols of bodhisattvas, manifesting the outward appearance of a layman, heard the name of the Tathāgata and leaped down from Abhirati.
Compassionate toward the suffering of sentient beings in the world, he manifested illness in the city of Vaiśālī. His myriad transformations arose from divine metamorphosis;
a single peck was like water poured from a jar. Now that you have struck upon the Dharma of non-duality, how could you remain silent and without sound?
The Fish-basket Maiden carries her basket of fish, presenting her powder-white face; she stirs the heart of the youth from the Ma family.
As the mountain shadows swirl before his dazzled eyes, he recites the seven fascicles of the Lotus Sutra to their end, begging for but a single string of golden bones.
The girl Lingzhao cast aside worldly affairs and trod upon the profound mechanism. Her father had no one to rely on; the daughter was even more headstrong.
Knowing full well that she was not as happy as the poor man who delights in his poverty, she deliberately went along the steps to sell her colanders.
Xuansha exchanged his head and left the Xie family; on the banks of the Nantai River, he has a life of plenty.
Dripping with putrid pus, no one understands—laughing until they fall over the white artemisia and red smartweed flowers.
The Boatman was the son of Yaoshan and the grandson of Shitou; hungry and with a wild mind, he rushed through the waves.
Having caught a magnificent scaled fish of such great size, it seems he should share it with Daowu.
Regarding the portrait of Master Yuanzhao, which Master Xi requested as a single brushstroke transmission—what kind of form does it take?
It resembles an imperial decree for an ancient king of trees; standing tall, it reaches out beyond the clouds.
It possesses not a single branch or leaf, yet it has a full ten parts of magnanimity. Truly, it is the model for the monastic community.
The Portrait of Master Shixi: Pai Tang requests:
This old monk possesses a most compassionate countenance; his pure shadow falls upon the human world, while his fragrant name permeates the heavens.

It polishes away flaws across the eight directions and brings forth the refined brilliance of the myriad phenomena. With its jagged rock ridges and shimmering stream reflections, this single brushstroke has been transmitted as a masterpiece beyond all other artisans.
At the summit of Lingxiao Peak, emerald-green cliffs are heaped together.
The true likeness of Dharma Master Fuguang was enshrined by the Librarian Zangzhu, who invited the eminent monks Ying, Jiao, Zhong, and Jie;
they donned the golden robes of the Song dynasty and wielded the wooden tongues of Tiantai and Suihang, like the Milky Way overturning.
Like a rock splitting asunder, withered flowers swept away by the wind, rain brings forth the new and strange. The lightning flash has already vanished, yet the thunder does not cease.

If one is a son of the five heinous crimes, seeing through to the bottom, penetrating clearly, and capturing it perfectly, one will know for certain that this old monk—what he has said in the past, what he says now, and what he shall say hereafter—is exactly thus.
White clouds push forth the full, round moon.

In praising myself, I originally possess no such form; I have merely painted a rigid image. It is like Mount Huading on Tiantai: whether shrouded in mist or bright in sunshine, its appearance shifts through many moods.
Even the exquisite brushwork of Gu Kaizhi and Lu Tanwei could only produce a likeness that is not truly it. To paint it as a likeness is to gaze upon its summit.
[The head] is tilted; it is more than forty-eight thousand *zhang* high.
To call this a sheer cliff is like driving a wedge into one’s eyes; to say it is not a sheer cliff is like reaching for the moon in water.
It cannot be drawn and cannot be seen through clearly—plainly, one wears the snows of the Himalayas upon one’s head.

Breaking through the azure void, shattering the precipitous cliffs—such a bearing as this, who could possibly accompany it? *Ei!* Nine Rocks Constantly Abiding requests that a single thread be made into a line;
with a solitary palm, he claps his hands, altering the pattern to paint a cat, thereby bringing all things into a single standard. He stirs it up...
The spring at Meng is thoroughly turbid; how can one avoid the yoke of a thousand catties at the nape of the neck?
Elder Zhuang of Jing-she invited [the Master], who was neither truly real nor truly false. From afar he sketched him out, shifting his double brows beneath his eyes.
Who is it that does this? It is the Pure Society of the Western Hills. One must strictly avoid mistaking a donkey for a horse.

At the Puyuan Hermitage in Hangzhou, they request flowers to be inserted into a branch that has not yet sprouted; they wear a seamless robe and roll an embroidered ball before a hundred thousand people—an eighty-year-old man.
The old man forgets his age; he pushes open the gate of the thousand sages. Heaven and earth are swallowed by a single hair; he presses through the Road of Chang’an.
Purity and defilement cannot withstand the sweeping of the broom. In years past, he once trod upon Mount Sumeru; now he perceives that all other mountains are small.
He spreads out the colors of blue and red and strikes them all around; the cat washes its face and says it is fine.
The portrait of the Elder Gaofeng Miao. Layman Shen Yi requested it, removing one and retaining seven.
Having shattered the mass of doubt—*du du du*!—he leapt onto Mount Tianmu and occupied the lion’s den.
With a graceful air of mastery, he cast his shadow back across the rivers and lakes; how joyful that our house has such a son!
Surpassing all the great Chan Buddhas of the world.
A verse on the stone wall.
The well cannot be drawn from, nor can it be pierced; how many times has the spring breeze grown the moss?
Though Zhaozhou’s staff is coarse and plain, it is doubtful he ever actually leaned upon it.
The mountains and rivers of the great earth in Hainan roll with surging waves. The lad of the south (Cíngdīng) squints his eyes;
turning his head, he strikes through the deep blue sea, and the barefooted Persian enters with ivory.
When the myriad functions of the single mountain have all ceased, the gates of the mouth are sealed; to call this "suchness" (tathatā) is already to fall into the secondary and tertiary.
Pressed until the entire body returns to the sheer cliff, Sudhana would not have reached it had he not gone to consult the other peak.
Question:
"When An struck the gate, did he knock? Zhaozhou used the staff to strike, failing to guard his own house; as before, he merely held up his fist.
It was not necessarily that mugwort soup could serve as tea.

Snowflakes fall, flake by flake, never landing elsewhere; they suddenly emerge from the precipice of the present moment. At this time, if you strike upon them, you are a guest of the "Mumbling Chan" (Nao Chan);
in such urgency, even Master Pang has not yet found his way home.
In an empty valley, one side merely calls and the other responds; ten thousand woodcutters pursue a hollow sound. Though they search, there is truly no trace to be found;
one sees only the green mountains, ever and ever green.
Dushan stands alone, washed by two winds and ground by solitude; towering and remote, the trees wither and their leaves fall, steep and majestic. This one matter alone admits of no admixture;
how could its vastness ever be concealed?
Resting my arm upon the pillow, I cast my entire body down and indulge in my folly. With elbows and arms clearly bent, toward whom do they point?
If you wish for further dreams within a dream, I have no wooden pillow for you to push.
At Yupu, one is received between Mount Wu and beyond Mount Yue; there is rice to satisfy hunger and a mat to sleep upon.
Though one may find rest here, the Imperial Capital remains separated by but a single tide’s journey by boat.

A thank-you note for the Dharma robe sent by Master Yuanzhao, the robe formerly kept by my elder brother, Master Kāśyapa: Its four borders are about to fly away like clouds; Xuefeng recognized it as an article of our own house.
With palms joined and head bowed, he received it and brought it back home.
Seeing off Head Seat Gong’s return to Wenzhou:
Where is there not moon over the river and wind through the pines? The precept-jewel and mind-seal are but forced names and models. I trouble you to ask Old Zhenjue upon your return:
Why is it that your breath, O Acharya, has not yet ceased?
A Zen guest presented an inquiry, asking, "What is the Master’s intention? A single phrase in response would already involve too much;
before the question has even finished its sound, it is already another question—unaware that the hawk has already flown over Silla.

The Layman Jing’an requested that I not write the character for "mind" upon his window-screen. Jade mixed with silt and sand, yet its essence remains distinct; Ten thousand anxieties are suddenly forgotten, and all impurities cease.
The azure sky is free of taint, and the water leaves no trace.
As I see off the attendant who returns to his hometown, I bid him farewell for the third time; he shall dwell on the Snowy Mountains. I play the stringless lute at every moment;
tonight, a single melody in the highest key flows forth like the eighteen rapids of the West River.
Sending Little Master Xinyin on His Journey:
Since first setting foot upon leaving the mother’s womb, How could this single seal have ever been lost? Before one's eyes, the spring mountains and spring waters are green;
Layer upon layer of seams—whose are they to open?
When Minister Manggu fashioned a golden stupa to enshrine the śarīra, he scattered six or seven mani-jewels beneath it;
the stūpa surged upward in thirteen tiers. Clearly, this single point of the central pivot has manifested—how could it have been forged from refined gold?
Entrusting this to the Reverend Shen Guangmo:
ten-thousand-fathom divine light washes away the world’s darkness; who knows who can believe that heaven and earth exist?
With so many venerable elders at the foot of the Three Mountains, which one will come to knock upon the gate of Old Guan?
The Great Vinaya Master (arriving from Mount Yangshan) finds Yangshan pushing aside his pillow to play with his cherished child.
Both are manifestations of great compassion displayed before the pivot of the occasion; why need one change one’s head to present a plain face?
Reapplying rouge and powder to paint the蛾眉 (arched brows).
I have stayed with the Elder Wushi at Xiufeng for three years;
though fish and wild geese have long been silent, our hearing remains clear. Although Min and Zhejiang are divided by geography, our minds remain undivided.
How many times have I stood before the wind, rubbing my aged eyes, and gazed coldly upon the clouds atop Mount Wushi?
A Minor Buddhist Rite for the West Hall Abbot’s Stupa: "Tou!
A Fellow Practitioner Succeeds Whomever: "The wooden sounding-block once struck east of Xiushui; last night, it suddenly turned elsewhere."
Tuned. Within the hollows of the skull, the pine wind roars; its lingering echoes trail on, leaving no trace behind. The green mountains cannot conceal it;
the bright moon perfectly accommodates it.
For the sake of the nation, the Pure and Vacant Venerable One raises his coffin to plant seeds in the depths of hell.
He releases the bed’s crossbow mechanism and drives a single arrow into Lake Tai; fish and dragons beg for their lives.

He spreads his *yaya* mat upon a more excellent seat, causing Han Shan and Shide to knit their brows. Riding backward upon the white-tigered beast, even the Buddha-eye cannot perceive him. Last night at the third watch—
Beyond the Iron Ring Mountains:
Chan the Rector’s fire; Xinghua beating Kebin;
sifting salt and wasting vinegar; Yunfeng hearing the bucket burst; receiving the resonance and inheriting the void; smashing it to pieces.
A double barrier. Having been restored to life from the midst of death, one should now cast oneself into the training of Shengre.

Linji served as attendant to Pingshan and took charge of Huangbo’s affairs; he repaid injustice with injustice. When Niaoke blew on a piece of cloth-hair, there was no calculating involved in his standing firm.
Calculating. A skull strikes the ground; the wise must know this. A wooden man holds a board and beats it amidst the clouds;
a stone woman holds a flute and blows it beneath the water.
Master Hui’s fire.
By day he does not leave the assembly; by night he does not leave the assembly. Wisdom is his essence, and meditative concentration is his function.

Although he is indeed a dead snake, throughout his life he has specialized in playing with him as if alive. With concentration and wisdom perfectly bright, he does not stagnate in emptiness. When a scorched brick strikes, it freezes through to the very bottom.

Ke, the steward, when the sky was clear and bright, harvested the grain; when the rain fell, he thatched the roof. The meaning of the Patriarchs is most clear: who can distinguish the melody when the string is plucked?
Morning drags on, evening is spent in toil; like extinguished embers without flame, they chase after emptiness. Good Ke, good Ke, watch over the fire!
Candle. Master Stone Mountain’s fire is as solitary and hard as stone;
his dignity is as weighty as a mountain. He overturns the vast ocean-treasury of Vairocana with a single step. Having arrived here, what [is there to say]?
This is called birth and death. What is called nirvana? One must recognize true gold by looking within the fire.
When Chan Master Zhan rose, his bones were ashy and his breath cold; the water was clear and the waves stilled. To settle and dwell here is to deceive the monks. Why? It is still not enough.
The journey from Caoxi is but half a month’s travel.

Master Tong of the Tripitaka Hall—his entire body is it, his whole person is it. It illuminates the past and the present; it penetrates to the very bone and marrow. As for all other teachings of the Great Tripitaka, they are likewise so.
When thoroughly wiping away the scabs and sores with paper, let them be carried by the wind into the deep clouds.
Knowing the guest-fire through the precepts, one perceives the host within the guest; sing the song of returning home. A pure practitioner does not enter nirvana; a breaker of the precepts...

O Bhikṣu, you shall not enter hell. Having passed through the two stages of smearing, where shall you make your home? You shall roam amidst masses of fire with hair upon your body, and roll in dust and sand with horns upon your head.

The newly ordained shave their heads with the three-inch iron of the Wheel-Turning King; its use never strikes a sharp edge, leaving not even a hair’s breadth of obstruction. It rekindles the light atop the crown.
Entrustment of the robe.
A single transmission at Mei Ling: this one move alone is as light as a goose feather, yet as heavy as a mountain. Opening one’s chest, one must go;
only then will the words proceed. Qilin snaps the golden tether.
To display blessings is to hang the temple plaque;
the teaching is the Buddha’s words, and Chan is the Buddha’s mind. The Buddhas of antiquity displayed this plaque to manifest the sprout of the mind;

the Buddhas of the present day complete this plaque to clarify the root of the words. Root and sprout are one body; mind and words share a common source. Thus, it truly attains the brilliance of the Milky Way swirling above.
The great earth widely opens the realm of longevity; phoenixes and peacocks fly and dance. At Shaolin, all leap for joy in the spring breeze;
all who see or hear are filled with joy and glory, realizing the inconceivable. Layer upon layer is the ocean of the Flower Treasury; everywhere is the gate of *dhāraṇī*.

Tracing its ultimate purpose, it was through the power of the original vow of the Great Meritorious One that this extraordinary excellence was attained. It is moved by the causal inspiration of the two Buddhas.
As for the single phrase inscribed upon this high plaque to mark this auspicious occasion—how shall it be proclaimed? "Venerating Grace" (Chong'en)—its grace is inexhaustible;
"Expanding Blessings" (Yanfu)—its blessings are infinite.
Bamian transmitted these Dharma words to Xiaoyan. Attendant Qi requested them, saying:
"The World-Honored One had secret words, which Kāśyapa did not conceal. This direct transmission is more virulent than a venomous insect. Upon reaching that point—
"Householder, can water be drunk? Thus, while there was Mi’an, there was also Xiao’an, just as the World-Honored One had Kāśyapa.
Once that smile broke through, the secret words became distorted; the direct descendants have no way to cover it up—this is the case for Attendant Siqi.
Regarding the accusation and denunciation [of me], I have therefore based my conclusion on the facts of the case:
[you] wrote the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* and the name "Śākyamuni" in blood, and spat blood at people; yet in the end, it turns out this was merely a rumor.
The "Sending of Words" (Songyu). Benchang the Rector received a deep, piercing prodding from the tips of [the Master’s] ten fingers;
it was written in a single stroke, neither blending ink nor following vermilion. Nevertheless, after all, whose words were being transmitted? Whose words were being sent?
As for the fourfold dharma-realm of the *Avataṃsaka*, in which of these realms could it be subsumed? Benchang began to harbor doubts and specifically requested that [the Master] point it out to him.
I said: "Have you not seen how the youth Sudhana visited fifty-three spiritual friends?
One person was recommended by another, until finally he was directed by Maitreya to see Mañjuśrī, and Mañjuśrī directed him to see the Buddha.
As for that which the Buddha pointed out—O masters with clear eyes, do not let it slip away!"
The Vice Minister Qian Dongyan’s transcription of the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāraṇī*. The Head Seat Yuan requested this sutra;
it is as firm as a vajra—how could it permit the pricking of a needle? Because of Xingsheng’s remark that it is "rare," twenty-seven doubts were aroused in people.
Gautama, out of compassion for sentient beings, dismantled it section by section. Vice Minister Dongyan has not forgotten this.
The essential meaning is as follows; I have therefore recorded it in writing so that the significance of each character may shine clearly. You must look closely with urgency.
Regarding the inscribed scrolls of the "Verses on the Golden Pagodas of the Various Mountains":
in the past, King Aśoka constructed eighty-four thousand pagodas to enshrine the relics of the Buddha Śākyamuni, consolidating the immeasurable [relics] into one. Now...
The Grand Chancellor commissioned a thirteen-story stūpa to enshrine the precious jewels of the various patriarchs; these are beyond measure.
To view the present through the lens of the past is just as it was to view the present through the lens of the past—all have flowed forth from right mindfulness;

how could there be any distinction between them? One must know that where they cannot be depicted, golden light blazes forth; where they cannot be painted, the jade-like shadow swirls in perfect circles. Thus it is.
"You are a ruler like Yao and Shun; your subjects are people like those of Yao and Shun—nothing more than this.
Regarding the scroll of verses by Jing-an, titled 'Tranquil Śamatha':
one who does not know what lies beyond the hermitage cannot realize its meaning. Once one has entered, however..."
Having entered, someone suddenly asked: "Do you permit me to advance further? He simply replied: "Go! You are right in the midst of the clamor.
This follows the two verses on the portrait of Chan Master Chuejue leaving the mountains and on Bodhidharma seeing the King of Liang.
Starving and freezing in the Snowy Mountains, he did not die; instead, his poison spread throughout the world, causing great harm to many.

It is a pity he did not encounter [the Buddha] at Mount Shao earlier. Is this to be condemned? Is this not to be condemned? Having crossed the seas and the Han River, he came to deceive the Eastern Lands with his leveling pretenses.
His compassion may have been like a drum, yet he turned his head in defeat due to his error regarding King Liang. Is this to be praised? Is this not to be praised?
Praise! For the Chan practitioner of Shang, I have inscribed this scroll for his departure.
At Mount Yangshan and Zhongfu, the Dharma path has now declined and the lineage of the masters has grown thin. All alike recommend Jiyun of Zhongfu as the sole leader of the Great River.
Step forward. As for those who practice meditation, they single-mindedly gaze upon and pay homage [to the teacher], yet they must still seek guidance from the elder.
Therefore, I say to them: "One person spreads his claws within an eagle's nest; another lays his body across the edge of a sword. To draw near is to lose one's heart and soul;
to even contemplate it is to have one's head split and forehead cracked. If you wish to approach intimately, you must first extricate the sword and overturn the nest."
It is not that there is no part for entry and practice; otherwise, one must strictly avoid letting skulls cover the ground.
*The Recorded Sayings of Master Jue'an* (End).
